result: The Global Typhoid Genomics Consortium aggregated 13,000 Typhi genomes from 65 studies and 5 unpublished datasets, representing the largest collection to date. After quality control (excluding 35 genomes with implausible assembly sizes), 12,965 high-quality genomes from 110 countries were analyzed, with the majority originating from Southern Asia (n=8,231).
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C29, C30, and C31 are directly supported by explicit statements in the manuscript and data presented in Tables 1-2. The quality control criteria (assembly size 4.5-5.5 Mbp) is clearly defined and applied, and the geographical distribution is documented with specific counts.

result: H58 lineage (genotype 4.3.1) is dominant in Southern Asia (70.4% prevalence) and Eastern Africa (93.3%), but has not spread to other regions where distinct genotypes dominate. Regional variation exists within Southern Asia, with H58 representing only 42% in Bangladesh compared to 94% in Pakistan. Outside Asia and Eastern/Southern Africa, genotypes 3.1.1 and 2.3.2 dominate in Western Africa, and 2.3.2 dominates in Central America.
evaluation: Claims C3, C4, and C32-C40 are well-supported by prevalence data presented in Figure 1 and the text, with specific percentages and confidence intervals provided for each region and country. The geographical restriction of H58 and the independent evolution of distinct genotypes in other regions is clearly demonstrated.

result: Ciprofloxacin non-susceptibility (CipNS) is widespread globally, emerging or established in all regions except Melanesia and in all well-sampled countries except Ghana. Ciprofloxacin resistance (CipR) is well-established across Southern Asia and emerging in Chile, Mexico, and South Africa.
evaluation: Claims C5, C41, C42, and C43 are supported by data in Figures 2 and 3, with specific prevalence rates provided. The widespread nature of CipNS and the more restricted distribution of CipR are clearly documented with statistical evidence.

result: High-level ciprofloxacin resistance (≥3 determinants) has reached 20% prevalence in South Asia, with 26 distinct CipR genotypes identified. The XDR strain 4.3.1.1.P1 accounts for 75% of Pakistani Typhi in 2020, while strain 4.3.1.3.Bdq accounts for 95% of CipR in Bangladesh, and 4.3.1.2.1 accounts for 92.3% of CipR in India.
evaluation: Claims C6, C44, C45, C46, C48, and C49 are supported by specific prevalence data in Figures 2-3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 5. The emergence and dominance of specific CipR strains in different countries is well-documented with temporal trends.

result: Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) typhoid (genotype 4.3.1.1.P1) has become dominant in Pakistan (70% in 2020, 87% by year-end), but has not established elsewhere. This study identifies that the XDR strain existed in Pakistan in July 2015 (strain Rwp1-PK1 from Rawalpindi), a full year earlier than previously reported outbreaks in Sindh Province in late 2016.
evaluation: Claims C7, C26, C27, C34, C52, C57-C60, and C102 are strongly supported by data in Figures 3-4 and phylogenetic analysis. The identification of Rwp1-PK1 from 2015 is a novel finding from this aggregated analysis, supported by genomic evidence (marker SNV, phylogenetic clustering, AMR determinants) and clinical data from the original report.

result: Ceftriaxone resistance has emerged in eight non-XDR genotypes through various ESBL genes. A notable sublineage of 4.3.1.2.1 carrying blaSHV-12 in an IncX3 plasmid has persisted in Mumbai from 2015-2020 (15 local isolates plus 3 travel-associated cases), but shows no evidence of spread beyond Maharashtra or India.
evaluation: Claims C8, C61, C62, C63, and C64 are supported by detailed data in Table 3 and accompanying text. The persistence of the Mumbai strain is documented through temporal and geographical distribution of isolates, though the inference of limited spread is based on absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence.

result: Azithromycin resistance (AziR) mutations in acrB were detected at low prevalence (74 genomes total) in South Asia, primarily in Bangladesh (n=55, 2.6% prevalence) and India (n=11, 0.5% prevalence). Thirteen distinct genotype-mutation combinations were identified, indicating at least 13 independent emergence events. Notably, 8 acrB mutants also carried ciprofloxacin resistance, including 6 in the CipR 4.3.1.2.1 lineage in India and 2 in the CipR 4.3.1.3.Bdq lineage.
evaluation: Claims C9, C28, C65-C73 are well-supported by data in Figure 5 and accompanying text. The low prevalence, multiple independent origins, and co-occurrence with CipR are clearly documented. The inference of independent emergence events from distinct genotype-mutation combinations is reasonable.

result: MDR prevalence has declined significantly in India (p=2×10⁻⁹) to 2% and in Bangladesh (p=2×10⁻⁴) but remains >20% in Bangladesh. MDR has remained high in Kenya and Malawi since H58 arrival, but declined in Nigeria from 72% (2009) to 10% (2017, p=3×10⁻⁴). Persistence of MDR in certain settings correlates with chromosomal integration of the MDR transposon (100% in Malawi, 19% in Kenya), which is associated with lower fitness cost compared to plasmid-borne MDR.
evaluation: Claims C50, C51, C53, C54, C55, C56, and C104 are supported by temporal trend data in Figure 3 with statistical tests (proportion trend tests with significant p-values). The correlation between MDR persistence and chromosomal integration is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, though the fitness cost explanation is based on cited literature rather than direct measurement in this study.

result: National genotype and AMR prevalence estimates from 2010-2020 were largely concordant between local surveillance studies and travel-associated cases captured elsewhere. In 67% of genotype-source combinations, individual laboratory estimates had 95% CIs overlapping with pooled national estimates. Notable exceptions included genotype 4.3.1.2 prevalence in India (ranging 16-82% across laboratories) and temporal differences in Nigeria (Abuja 2010-2013 vs Ibadan 2017-2018).
evaluation: Claims C74-C83, C88, and C89 are supported by detailed comparisons in Figures 6-7 and supplements. The concordance analysis is methodologically sound, using 95% CI overlap as the criterion. The exceptions are well-documented and explained (geographical variation in India, temporal differences in Nigeria). This demonstrates that travel-associated data can be informative for surveillance.

result: The study has important limitations, including scarcity of genomic data from many endemic regions (Northern and Middle Africa, Western Asia, Central and South America), reflecting underlying lack of routine blood culture surveillance and limited resources. For some countries and regions, travel-associated data represented most or all available genome data, and routine sequencing of travel-associated infections in high-income countries helps fill surveillance gaps.
evaluation: Claims C84-C87 are explicitly acknowledged limitations supported by data gaps shown in Tables 1-2 and Supplementary files. The reliance on travel-associated data for certain regions is documented, and the utility of such data is demonstrated by the concordance analysis (C88-C89).

result: The WHO has prequalified two TCVs and recommended their use in endemic countries and settings with high AMR prevalence. Gavi has committed funds for TCV procurement and distribution, with five countries undertaking Gavi-supported national introductions (Pakistan, Liberia, Zimbabwe, Nepal, Malawi) and one self-financed (Samoa). In Pakistan and Zimbabwe, TCV introduction was stimulated by AMR Typhi outbreaks. TCVs have been shown to be highly effective against drug-resistant Typhi.
evaluation: Claims C90-C94 are supported by citations to WHO and Gavi sources, and published effectiveness studies. These are factual statements about policy and vaccine effectiveness, appropriately cited.

result: The WHO AWaRe treatment guidelines indicate that empiric therapy choice should be guided by severity and local fluoroquinolone resistance risk. If low risk, oral ciprofloxacin is recommended for both mild and severe cases; if high risk, oral azithromycin for mild cases and IV ceftriaxone for severe cases. However, the guidelines do not specify which resistance prevalence rate should warrant avoidance of ciprofloxacin, nor where high prevalence is expected.
evaluation: Claims C95-C98 accurately describe the WHO AWaRe guidelines with appropriate citation, and correctly identify a limitation (lack of specific prevalence thresholds). This is a factual description of existing guidelines.

result: This study provides an analytical framework for Typhi genomic analysis using open-access platforms (Typhi Mykrobe, GHRU pipeline, Typhi Pathogenwatch), with all data processing code, statistical analysis code, and underlying data made available via GitHub and FigShare. The consortium-driven aggregated analysis revealed new insights not evident from individual studies, including persistence of the CefR+CipR strain in Mumbai (2015-2020) now identified as 4.3.1.2.1 with blaSHV-12.
evaluation: Claims C99, C100, C101, and C103 are supported by explicit statements about methods and data availability, with appropriate citations to the tools used. The value of aggregated analysis is demonstrated by specific examples of new insights (C102, C103, C104).

result: This dataset provides actionable information about AMR distribution and temporal trends across multiple countries and regions. The authors recommend that these data should inform prioritization of TCV introduction and WASH infrastructure improvements, and that sustaining genomic surveillance can facilitate measuring TCV impact on bacterial populations and monitoring for potential strain replacement with other Salmonella serovars.
evaluation: Claims C105-C108 represent recommendations and future directions rather than demonstrated results. While C105 is supported by the data presented, C106-C108 are speculative recommendations about how the data should be used and what future surveillance could achieve. These are reasonable suggestions but not empirically validated in this study.

result: Background context on typhoid burden, mortality, antimicrobial resistance history, and genomic framework development. This includes historical information about typhoid epidemiology (10.9 million illnesses, 116,800 deaths in 2017), mortality rates (pre-antibiotic era 10-20% vs <1% today), emergence of MDR in the 1970s, the first Typhi genome sequence in 2001, evolutionary rate (~0.5 substitutions/year), and the GenoTyphi framework development.
evaluation: Claims C10-C25 are background information appropriately cited to published literature (GBD 2017, Parkhill et al. 2001, Wong et al. 2016a, etc.). These establish context for the current study and are supported by the cited sources.
